absent: Dispatch queue creation, identifier allocation, and full user queue lifetime beyond lookup, iteration, peek, requeue, and destroy.
Scheduler object layout and resolution from program auxiliary context, plus scheduler registration and teardown.
Runqueue and per-processor local queue structures, kick wakeup effects, and dispatch selection behavior.
Compute identifier to processor translation table setup, updates, and offline handling.
Event counter definitions, update sites, and cgroup weight or bandwidth effects.
Exit claim and finish transitions, dump session setup, and performance target application to hardware.

findings.text: Provides a scheduler callable that records a virtual time value on a task already associated with the invoking scheduler, reporting success only when the scheduler resolves and the task belongs to it.

Offers scheduler callables to request prompt reconsideration of a specified processor, directly by processor number or indirectly through a compute identifier that is translated first, quietly ignoring unknown schedulers or invalid targets.

Reports how many tasks are queued for a dispatch queue identifier, handling the current local queue, a named per-processor local queue, and user queues, with distinct negative signals for a missing scheduler versus an unknown queue.
Exposes teardown of a dispatch queue selected by identifier whenever the scheduler for the invoking program can be resolved.

Defines a three-phase traversal over a user dispatch queue where creation validates flags and queue existence, stepping yields successive tasks under queue protection, and teardown detaches the cursor and clears the association.
Returns the first queued task of a user dispatch queue without removing it, treating builtin queues and unknown identifiers as scheduler errors that yield no task.

Requeues the contents of a chosen dispatch queue according to caller filter bits, defaulting to an any-match when no filter is supplied and rejecting unknown flag bits, with a convenience wrapper that targets the local queue.

Provides formatted scheduler termination, error reporting, and dump-append operations on top of a shared formatter that validates argument size, copies arguments safely, prepares and renders the message, with dump restricted to the dumping processor and supporting multi-call line accumulation.

Supplies read-only performance capability and current performance level for a processor or compute identifier, falling back to a normalized unity value when scheduler resolution, identifier translation, or processor validation fails.

Allows setting a per-processor performance target with upper-bound validation, processor validity checks, refusal of cross-processor updates while a different runqueue is held, and denial when the needed capability is missing.

Exposes topology sizes and masks including node count, processor identifier count, possible and online compute identifier counts, the current compute identifier, an online compute mask translated for scheduler access, and global possible and online processor masks with a no-op release for trusted pointer handling.

Exposes task placement and execution state such as whether a task is currently executing, its processor, its compute identifier through a shared translation table, the currently locked runqueue, and current tasks selected by processor or identifier.

Provides thread identifier lookup gated by an enable flag and hash table, a scheduler time source usable across process and interrupt contexts, a size-tolerant event statistics copy, and reference-counted task cgroup resolution limited to tasks under operation.

Every scheduler-aware helper resolves its scheduler from the invoking program context and treats absence as failure using the helper-appropriate signal such as false, null, or a negative status, with kick and destroy helpers simply doing nothing.

Dispatch queue identifiers partition into a current-local selector, per-processor local selectors distinguished by embedded bits, builtin queues marked by a flag bit, and user queues found by exact identifier lookup.
Task-scoped helpers accept only tasks currently under operation by the caller and otherwise report a scheduler error and take the failure path.

Each scheduler operation permits only a defined subset of helper classes, with unlocked operations allowing only unlocked helpers, execution-path operations allowing enqueue or dispatch helpers, and special allowances for processor release and identifier initialization.
Requeue with no filter bits behaves the same as requesting any-match, and performance queries return unity whenever validation cannot be completed.
Most scheduler helpers hold read-side RCU protection while resolving the scheduler and while dereferencing shared pointers such as translation tables, current tasks, and queue heads.

Queue-length queries and time, event, and exit paths run with preemption controlled, while performance updates and locked-runqueue access coordinate with runqueue locking and refuse cross-processor updates when a different runqueue is already held.
Iteration stepping and teardown synchronize cursor movement and list detachment under the target dispatch queue lock with interrupt state preserved.
Kernel iterator state is required to fit within the user-visible iterator footprint with identical alignment, and reserves flag space that does not overlap node-private bits.
Exit reporting uses a fixed-size message area with fallback diagnostic text when formatting fails, and dump reporting appends into a shared line buffer with a bounded cursor clamped at capacity.
Iterator state starts empty, becomes bound to a user queue on successful creation, stays bound across stepping calls, and returns to empty after explicit teardown or when creation fails.
Exit handling claims the exit exactly once, attempts message formatting with substitution of diagnostic text on failure, then finalizes with kind, code, and processor identity.
Dump accumulation retains partial line content across calls and flushes into the dump when the buffer fills or ends with a newline.
The file registers a scheduler helper set filtered by operation context, making the listed helpers invocable from scheduler programs subject to the allow matrix.

Invalid uses such as peeking builtin or missing queues, bad requeue flags, oversized performance targets, cross-processor updates under lock, dump calls from a non-dumping processor, or task arguments outside the current operation are reported as scheduler errors rather than proceeding.

Event copying and formatted-message handling tolerate caller size differences by copying the smaller of caller and native sizes and by validating argument byte length alignment and bounds before copying.

A constant named SCX_DSQ_LOCAL selects the current local queue. A base named SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_ON with a mask named SCX_DSQ_LOCAL_CPU_MASK selects a named processor local. A flag named SCX_DSQ_FLAG_BUILTIN marks builtin queues that peek must reject.
A mask named __SCX_REENQ_USER_MASK defines accepted requeue bits. A subset named __SCX_REENQ_FILTER_MASK defines filter bits. A value named SCX_REENQ_ANY supplies the default when no filter is given.

A mask named __SCX_DSQ_ITER_USER_FLAGS defines accepted iterator flags. A companion named __SCX_DSQ_ITER_ALL_FLAGS with a shift named __SCX_DSQ_LNODE_PRIV_SHIFT keeps iterator flags disjoint from node-private bits.

A value named SCX_CPUPERF_ONE normalizes performance levels and serves as fallback. A kind named SCX_EXIT_UNREG_BPF marks voluntary unregister exits. A kind named SCX_EXIT_ERROR_BPF marks error exits.

A capability named SCX_CAP_PERF gates performance updates. A counter named SCX_EV_SUB_CIDPERF_DENIED records denials. A length named SCX_EXIT_MSG_LEN bounds exit text. A count named MAX_BPRINTF_VARARGS bounds formatted arguments. A flag named SCX_OPS_TID_TO_TASK gates identifier lookup.
Six allow bits gate helper use by context. One named SCX_KF_ALLOW_UNLOCKED covers unlocked operations. Others cover selection, enqueue, dispatch, release, and identifier initialization respectively.

Negative statuses distinguish failure causes. One signals a missing scheduler device. Another signals an unknown queue. Another signals an invalid argument. Another signals a denied capability update.
